facts.one_liner: Osaka Castle’s keep rises above its stone walls and moat, with modern towers behind.
facts.why_go: Osaka is Japan’s third-largest city and its street-food capital, known for the motto kuidaore—‘eat until you drop’. Osaka Castle, rebuilt in concrete in 1931 on the site of Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s 16th-century fortress, stands in a large park ringed by massive stone walls and moats. After dark, head to Dōtonbori’s neon canal for takoyaki and okonomiyaki, explore the retro Shinsekai district, and use the city as a base for day trips to Kyoto, Nara and Kobe.
facts.best_time: Late March–early April for cherry blossoms around the castle and October–November for autumn colour. Summers are hot and humid.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Kansai International (KIX); the Nankai and JR trains reach the city in about 40–50 minutes. Itami (ITM) handles domestic flights. Shinkansen trains stop at Shin-Osaka; the subway covers the city.
facts.good_to_know: An IC card (ICOCA, Suica) works on trains, subways and convenience stores. The castle grounds are free; the museum inside the keep charges admission.

facts.one_liner: The tiled Bab Bou Jeloud gate frames a minaret at the entrance to the Fes medina.
facts.why_go: Fez is Morocco’s oldest imperial city and its spiritual and craft capital. Fes el-Bali, its walled medina, is a UNESCO World Heritage site and one of the largest car-free urban areas in the world—a maze of thousands of lanes where donkeys still carry goods. Enter through the blue-and-green tiled Bab Bou Jeloud, visit the Al Quaraouiyine mosque-university founded in 859, watch dyers at the Chouara tannery from surrounding terraces, and stay in a restored riad with a tiled courtyard.
facts.best_time: March–May and September–November for pleasant temperatures. Summers are very hot; winters can be cold and wet.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Fès–Saïss Airport (FEZ), about 20–30 minutes from the medina, or take ONCF trains from Casablanca, Rabat or Tangier. Petit taxis run between the new town and medina gates.
facts.good_to_know: Hire an official licensed guide for your first medina visit—it is easy to get lost. Dress modestly; non-Muslims cannot enter most mosques.

facts.one_liner: Pastel colonial houses and church towers slope down the cobbled Largo do Pelourinho.
facts.why_go: Salvador was Brazil’s first capital (1549–1763) and is the heart of Afro-Brazilian culture. Its Pelourinho historic centre, a UNESCO World Heritage site, climbs the hills of the upper city with pastel colonial houses and gold-filled baroque churches such as São Francisco. Ride the Elevador Lacerda between the upper and lower towns, watch capoeira and drum groups like Olodum, eat acarajé from Bahian street vendors, and swim at beaches such as Porto da Barra—especially during Salvador’s enormous street Carnival.
facts.best_time: September–March for sunnier, drier weather; Carnival is in February or March. April–July is the rainiest period.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Salvador International (SSA), about 30–45 minutes from the centre by taxi or metro connection. Use taxis or ride-hailing at night.
facts.good_to_know: Stay alert in quiet streets after dark, and keep valuables out of sight. Book well ahead for Carnival.

facts.one_liner: The Space Needle rises over Seattle with snow-capped Mount Rainier glowing behind.
facts.why_go: Seattle sits between Puget Sound and Lake Washington with the Cascade Mountains and Mount Rainier on the horizon. The 184-metre Space Needle, built for the 1962 World’s Fair, has a revolving glass floor and observation deck. Watch fish fly at Pike Place Market, ride a ferry to Bainbridge Island for skyline views, visit the Chihuly Garden and Glass and Museum of Pop Culture, and tour the coffee shops of the city that launched Starbucks.
facts.best_time: July–September for dry, sunny, mild weather and the best mountain views. October–May is cool and often drizzly.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Seattle–Tacoma International (SEA); Link light rail reaches downtown in about 40 minutes. Amtrak connects from Portland and Vancouver. Ferries cross Puget Sound from the downtown terminal.
facts.good_to_know: Mount Rainier is only visible on clear days—check the forecast before heading up the Needle. A CityPASS covers several major attractions.

facts.one_liner: The Las Vegas Strip blazes with lights from end to end at night.
facts.why_go: Las Vegas rose from the Mojave Desert as America’s entertainment capital, and the Strip is its 4-mile parade of themed mega-resorts, casinos and stage shows. Watch the Bellagio’s dancing fountains, catch a residency or Cirque du Soleil show, eat at celebrity-chef restaurants and see the vintage neon of Downtown’s Fremont Street and the Neon Museum. Beyond the lights, Red Rock Canyon is about 30 minutes away, the Hoover Dam about 45 minutes, and the Grand Canyon is within a day trip.
facts.best_time: March–May and October–November for warm, pleasant days. Summer regularly exceeds 40°C (104°F); winter nights are cool.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Harry Reid International (LAS), just a few minutes from the south end of the Strip. The Las Vegas Monorail runs behind several Strip resorts; buses and ride-hailing cover the rest.
facts.good_to_know: Distances on the Strip are longer than they look—wear comfortable shoes and drink water in the heat. Resort fees are added to many hotel rates.

facts.one_liner: Ljubljana Castle crowns a wooded hill above the red roofs of Slovenia’s capital.
facts.why_go: Ljubljana is a small, green and largely car-free capital along the Ljubljanica River, shaped by architect Jože Plečnik, whose Triple Bridge, riverside market colonnades and National Library define its look. Ljubljana Castle crowns the hill above the old town and is reached by a funicular. Spend lazy hours at riverside cafés, browse the Central Market, explore Tivoli Park, and use the city as a base for Lake Bled, Postojna Cave and the Julian Alps.
facts.best_time: May–September for outdoor café life and festivals; December for festive lights. Spring and autumn are mild and quiet.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Ljubljana Jože Pučnik Airport (LJU), about 30 minutes by shuttle or bus. Trains and buses connect to Zagreb, Vienna, Trieste and Venice. The centre is walkable.
facts.good_to_know: Much of the old town is pedestrian only; free electric shuttles (Kavalir) carry visitors. The funicular is the easy way up to the castle.

facts.one_liner: Gdańsk’s gabled merchants’ houses and the medieval crane line the Motława River waterfront.
facts.why_go: Gdańsk is a Baltic port city with a thousand-year history as a Hanseatic trading hub, painstakingly rebuilt after World War II. Its Main Town is lined with tall, colourful merchants’ houses; the Long Market and Neptune’s Fountain lead to the riverside Long Embankment and the medieval wooden port crane. It is also where World War II began at Westerplatte and where the Solidarity movement started at the shipyard—now home to the European Solidarity Centre. Amber shops line Mariacka Street.
facts.best_time: May–September for long days and Baltic beaches (August brings St Dominic’s Fair). Winter is cold but has Christmas markets.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Gdańsk Lech Wałęsa Airport (GDN), about 30 minutes from the old town by train, bus or taxi. Trains connect to Warsaw in about 3 hours. The old town is walkable.
facts.good_to_know: Combine Gdańsk with Sopot and Gdynia (the ‘Tricity’) by SKM commuter train. Climb St Mary’s Basilica tower or the Town Hall tower for rooftop views.

Named after the nearby St. Peter's Chapel, th

facts.one_liner: The covered wooden Chapel Bridge and its octagonal water tower cross the Reuss in Lucerne.
facts.why_go: Lucerne sits where the Reuss River leaves Lake Lucerne, with mountains such as Pilatus and Rigi rising nearby. The covered wooden Kapellbrücke (Chapel Bridge), first built in the 14th century and restored after a 1993 fire, crosses the river beside its stone water tower. Wander the painted facades of the old town, see the Lion Monument carved into a cliff, take a paddle steamer across the lake, and ride the cogwheel railway or cable cars up Mount Pilatus.
facts.best_time: May–October for lake cruises and mountain excursions. December has Christmas markets; spring and autumn are quieter.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Zurich Airport (ZRH), then take a train to Lucerne (about 1 hour). The station is right by the lake and old town. Boats, buses and mountain railways cover the region.
facts.good_to_know: Swiss Travel Pass holders get free boat travel and discounts on many mountain railways—check current inclusions. Mountain-top views depend on weather; check webcams before heading up.

facts.one_liner: The eye-shaped Hemisfèric glows over its reflecting pool in Valencia’s City of Arts and Sciences.
facts.why_go: Valencia, Spain’s third-largest city, combines a historic centre with Mediterranean beaches and bold modern architecture. The City of Arts and Sciences—a futuristic complex by Santiago Calatrava and Félix Candela—includes the Hemisfèric, science museum, opera house and Europe’s largest aquarium. It sits in the Turia Gardens, a 9-km park built in a former riverbed. Eat paella where it was born, see the silk exchange (La Lonja, UNESCO-listed) and the Central Market, and visit in March for the fiery Fallas festival.
facts.best_time: April–June and September–October for warm days without the summer peak. Las Fallas runs in mid-March; July–August is hot and busy at the beaches.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Valencia Airport (VLC); Metro lines 3 and 5 reach the centre in about 20–25 minutes. High-speed trains from Madrid take about 2 hours. Bikes and metro connect the old town, Turia Gardens and beach.
facts.good_to_know: Book Hemisfèric, science museum and Oceanogràfic tickets together for a discount. Traditional paella is a lunch dish—many locals eat it on Sundays.

facts.one_liner: The 18th-century Place de la Bourse reflected in the Miroir d’Eau on Bordeaux’s riverfront.
facts.why_go: Bordeaux, capital of the world’s most famous wine region, has a grand 18th-century core so intact that much of the city is a UNESCO World Heritage site (‘Port of the Moon’). The Place de la Bourse faces the Garonne, and in front of it the Miroir d’Eau, the world’s largest reflecting pool, alternates between a thin film of water and mist. Explore the Cité du Vin museum, café-lined squares and markets, and take day trips to vineyards in Saint-Émilion, the Médoc and Pessac-Léognan.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for pleasant weather—September and October bring the grape harvest. Summers can be hot.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Bordeaux–Mérignac (BOD), about 30–45 minutes from the centre by shuttle bus or tram. TGV trains from Paris take about 2 hours. Trams make getting around easy.
facts.good_to_know: Many châteaux require advance booking for tours and tastings. The Miroir d’Eau usually operates in the warmer months—check the season.

facts.one_liner: Palaces and temples rise above stepped ghats along the sacred Ganges at Varanasi.
facts.why_go: Varanasi, on the banks of the Ganges, is one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities and Hinduism’s holiest. Its riverfront is lined with more than 80 ghats—stone steps where pilgrims bathe, pray and, at Manikarnika and Harishchandra, cremate the dead. Take a dawn boat ride as the sun rises over the river, watch the evening Ganga Aarti fire ceremony at Dashashwamedh Ghat, wander the labyrinthine lanes of the old city, and visit Sarnath nearby, where the Buddha gave his first sermon.
facts.best_time: October–March for cooler, dry weather; Dev Deepawali (usually November) lights the ghats with lamps. April–June is extremely hot; July–September is monsoon.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Lal Bahadur Shastri Airport (VNS), about 45–60 minutes from the ghats by taxi. Trains connect to Delhi and Kolkata. Walk or take boats along the ghats; cycle-rickshaws and autos handle short hops.
facts.good_to_know: Be respectful at cremation ghats—don’t photograph funerals. Lanes are crowded and confusing; a local guide helps on your first day.

facts.one_liner: Nice’s Baie des Anges curves past the Promenade des Anglais, seen from Castle Hill.
facts.why_go: Nice is the capital of the French Riviera, set on the sweeping Baie des Anges where the Alps meet the Mediterranean. The Promenade des Anglais runs along the pebble beaches, and the Colline du Château (Castle Hill) gives the classic view over the bay and the red roofs of Vieux Nice. Browse the flower and produce market on Cours Saleya, eat socca and pissaladière, visit the Matisse and Chagall museums, and hop along the coast to Villefranche, Èze and Monaco by bus or train.
facts.best_time: May–June and September–October for warm sea and fewer crowds. The Nice Carnival takes place in February; July–August is hot and busy.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Nice Côte d’Azur Airport (NCE); tram line 2 reaches the centre in about 25 minutes. TGV and regional TER trains run along the coast. Trams, buses and walking cover the city.
facts.good_to_know: The beaches are pebbly—water shoes help. Climb Castle Hill (or take the lift) for sunset views.

facts.one_liner: A colonial sentry box on Cartagena’s sea walls silhouetted against a Caribbean sunset.
facts.why_go: Cartagena de Indias was a key Spanish colonial port, and its walled city and fortifications—including the massive Castillo San Felipe de Barajas—are a UNESCO World Heritage site. Inside the walls, bougainvillea spills from balconies over cobbled streets and colourful plazas. Walk the ramparts at sunset, explore the street-art and nightlife of Getsemaní, take a boat to the Rosario Islands’ beaches, and cool off with fresh fruit juices and ceviche.
facts.best_time: December–April is the dry season with sunny, breezy days. It is hot and humid year-round; October–November is the wettest period.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Rafael Núñez International (CTG), about 15 minutes by taxi from the walled city. Boats to the Rosario Islands leave from the Muelle de la Bodeguita.
facts.good_to_know: Midday heat is intense—explore early morning and late afternoon. Agree on taxi fares before getting in.

facts.one_liner: The Jesuit church of La Compañía faces the arcaded Plaza de Armas in Cusco.
facts.why_go: Cusco was the capital of the Inca Empire, and the Spanish built their churches and mansions on top of its finely fitted Inca stone walls—the whole city is a UNESCO World Heritage site. The Plaza de Armas is flanked by the cathedral and the ornate Jesuit Church of La Compañía. Explore the Qorikancha sun temple, the hilltop fortress of Sacsayhuamán, and the bohemian San Blas quarter, then use Cusco as the gateway to the Sacred Valley and Machu Picchu.
facts.best_time: May–September is the dry season with sunny days and cold nights. November–March brings rain; the Inca Trail closes in February.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Alejandro Velasco Astete International (CUZ), about 15–20 minutes from the centre by taxi; most flights connect via Lima. Trains to Machu Picchu leave from Poroy or Ollantaytambo.
facts.good_to_know: Cusco sits at about 3,400 m—take it easy on day one and drink plenty of water. The Boleto Turístico covers many sites around the region.

facts.one_liner: The cream-and-pink Chandra Mahal rises over a courtyard of Jaipur’s City Palace.
facts.why_go: Jaipur, Rajasthan’s capital, is the ‘Pink City’—its old town was painted terracotta pink to welcome the Prince of Wales in 1876, and the walled city is a UNESCO World Heritage site. The City Palace, still partly home to the royal family, centres on the seven-storey Chandra Mahal. Nearby are the honeycombed Hawa Mahal, the Jantar Mantar observatory (also UNESCO-listed) and the hilltop Amber Fort. Shop for block-printed textiles and gems in the bazaars and end the day at Nahargarh Fort for sunset.
facts.best_time: October–March for cool, dry weather. April–June is very hot, and July–September is monsoon season.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Jaipur International (JAI), about 30 minutes from the old city. Trains and expressways link it to Delhi and Agra as part of the ‘Golden Triangle’. Use taxis, autos or ride-hailing in town.
facts.good_to_know: A composite ticket covers several monuments, including Amber Fort and Hawa Mahal. Bargain in the bazaars and agree on auto fares first.

facts.one_liner: Pagoda-roofed temples crowd Kathmandu Durbar Square in the heart of the old city.
facts.why_go: Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, sits in a valley whose seven monument zones—including Kathmandu, Patan and Bhaktapur Durbar Squares, Swayambhunath, Boudhanath and Pashupatinath—form a UNESCO World Heritage site. Durbar Square’s tiered Newar temples and royal palace were damaged in the 2015 earthquake and many have been restored. Climb to the ‘Monkey Temple’ of Swayambhunath, circle the giant stupa of Boudhanath with pilgrims, eat momo dumplings, and gear up in Thamel for Himalayan treks.
facts.best_time: October–November for clear mountain views and festivals; March–April for rhododendron season. June–September is monsoon.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Tribhuvan International (KTM), about 20–30 minutes from Thamel by taxi. Domestic flights go to Pokhara and Lukla. Taxis and walking are the main ways around the city.
facts.good_to_know: Foreign visitors pay an entry fee for Durbar Square and other heritage zones. Air quality can be poor—consider a mask on dusty days.

facts.one_liner: A steep colonial street in old Quito climbs toward hills and church domes.
facts.why_go: Quito sits at about 2,850 m in an Andean valley beneath the Pichincha volcano, and in 1978 it was among the very first places inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage sites, thanks to one of Latin America’s best-preserved colonial centres. Stroll Plaza Grande and the baroque churches—La Compañía’s interior is covered in gold leaf—climb the towers of the neo-Gothic Basílica del Voto Nacional, ride the TelefériQo up the volcano’s slopes, and visit the equator monument at Mitad del Mundo.
facts.best_time: June–September is the drier season with sunny mornings. Quito has spring-like weather year-round, with afternoon showers common in other months.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Mariscal Sucre International (UIO), about 45–60 minutes from the centre by taxi or airport bus. Taxis are inexpensive; the Quito Metro opened in 2023.
facts.good_to_know: Take time to adjust to the altitude. Use registered taxis at night, especially around the old town.

facts.one_liner: Colourful colonial facades and a tiled church dome line a street in Oaxaca City.
facts.why_go: Oaxaca de Juárez is the capital of one of Mexico’s most culturally rich states, and its historic centre and the nearby Zapotec city of Monte Albán together form a UNESCO World Heritage site. Pastel colonial streets lead to the gilded Santo Domingo church and its botanical garden. Oaxaca is a food capital—try the many moles, tlayudas and chocolate—and the home of mezcal. Visit the Guelaguetza dance festival in July or the Día de Muertos celebrations around 1–2 November.
facts.best_time: October–April for dry, sunny weather; late October–early November for Día de Muertos. The rainy season is roughly June–September.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Oaxaca International (OAX), about 20–30 minutes from the centre. Buses connect from Mexico City (around 6–7 hours). The centre is compact and walkable; colectivos serve nearby villages.
facts.good_to_know: Book early for Guelaguetza and Día de Muertos. Monte Albán is a short drive or bus ride uphill from town.

facts.one_liner: The Bay of Naples and its busy port spread out beneath the cone of Mount Vesuvius.
facts.why_go: Naples is southern Italy’s great city: loud, layered and gloriously unpolished, with a UNESCO-listed historic centre built on a Greek and Roman street grid. It is the birthplace of pizza—try a margherita in the old town—and home to the National Archaeological Museum’s treasures from Pompeii. Explore Spaccanapoli’s churches and alleys, the underground tunnels of Napoli Sotterranea, and the waterfront Castel dell’Ovo, then day-trip to Pompeii, Herculaneum, Vesuvius and the Amalfi Coast or Capri.
facts.best_time: April–June and September–October for warm weather. July–August is hot and crowded; winter is mild.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Naples International (NAP), about 20 minutes from the centre by Alibus shuttle. High-speed trains from Rome take about 1–1.5 hours. Ferries leave for Capri and Ischia; the Circumvesuviana railway serves Pompeii and Herculaneum.
facts.good_to_know: Watch your belongings in crowded areas and on public transport. The ArteCard covers transport and museum discounts.

facts.one_liner: The Narikala fortress and the old town’s balconied houses glow at dusk above the Kura River.
facts.why_go: Tbilisi, Georgia’s capital, sprawls along the Mtkvari (Kura) River below the ancient Narikala fortress. Its old town mixes carved wooden balconies, Orthodox churches, mosques and the brick domes of the Abanotubani sulphur baths, where you can soak in naturally hot water. Ride the cable car up to the fortress, see the Bridge of Peace’s glass curve, and settle in for Georgian feasts of khachapuri, khinkali and amber wines made in clay qvevri, a UNESCO-listed tradition.
facts.best_time: April–June and September–October for warm, pleasant weather and the grape harvest (rtveli). Summers can be hot; winters are mild-to-cool.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly into Tbilisi International (TBS), about 20–30 minutes from the centre by taxi or bus. The metro, buses and inexpensive taxis cover the city.
facts.good_to_know: The old town is hilly—wear sturdy shoes. Book a private room at the sulphur baths, especially on weekends.
